blocks.text: On the bird כוס chos it is doubted whether it is a species of night bird, namely the eagle owl, the little owl, the owl, the night raven, or, very different from these, the onocrotalus.

The bird כוס chos, which follows next, is named only in the Law among the forbidden birds, and in Psalm. CII, 7, where the Psalmist says הייתי ככוס חרבות, I was like the chos of the wastes. And the Elders: Ἐγενήθην ὡσεὶ νυκτικόραξ ἐν οἰκοπέδῳ [Egenēthēn hōsei nyktikorax en oikopedō], I was like the night raven among ruined walls. Consulted about this passage by Sunia and Fretela, Jerome replies thus in his 135th Epistle: "You ask what nycticorax means among the Latins. In the Hebrew, in place of nycticorax, the word כוס chos is written, which Aquila, and the Seventy, and Theodotion, and the Fifth edition rendered night raven; Symmachus, however, hoopoe; the Sixth edition, little owl, which we too rather follow." And a little later: Most contend that it means eagle owl. Yet he himself, siding with them, renders it eagle owl both in the Law [col. 273] and in the Psalms.

The Arabs render it البوم [al-būm] album, that is, little owl. This is clear from the description of the album in Damir: البوم طاير يقع علي الذكر والانثي حتي تقول صدي او فياد فيتخص بالذكر وكنية الانثي ام الخراب وام الصيبان ويقال لها غراب الليل ومن طبعها انها تدخل علي كل طاير في وكره ليلا وتخرجه منه وتاكل فراخه وبيضه وهي قوية السلطان بالليل لا يحملها شي من الطير واذا راها الطير بالنهار قتلوها ونتفوا ريشها للعداوة التي بينهم وبينها ومن اجل ذلك صار الصياد يجعلها تحت شبكته لتقع الطير عليها [al-būm ṭāyir yaqaʿu ʿalā al-dhakar wa-al-unthā ḥattā taqūla ṣadā aw fayyād fa-yatakhaṣṣaṣu bi-al-dhakar wa-kunyat al-unthā umm al-kharāb wa-umm al-ṣībān wa-yuqālu lahā ghurāb al-layl wa-min ṭabʿihā annahā tadkhulu ʿalā kull ṭāyir fī wakrihi laylan wa-tukhrijuhu minhu wa-taʾkulu firākhahu wa-bayḍahu wa-hiya qawiyyat al-sulṭān bi-al-layl lā yaḥmiluhā shayʾ min al-ṭayr wa-idhā raʾāhā al-ṭayr bi-al-nahār qatalūhā wa-natafū rīshahā li-al-ʿadāwa allatī baynahum wa-baynahā wa-min ajl dhālika ṣāra al-ṣayyād yajʿaluhā taḥta shabakatihi li-taqaʿa al-ṭayr ʿalayhā]. Album is a bird. The name is of common gender; but if you say tsada or phajad, it will be proper to the male. The female's by-names are mother of the wasteland and mother of nits (because she swarms with them). It is also called raven of the night (that is, night raven). It is its nature to enter the nests of all birds by night and drive them out of them, so as to feed on their chicks and eggs. For by night it is so strong that no bird can withstand it; but the birds in turn attack it when they see it by day, and pluck its feathers, because of the hatred with which they pursue each other. Hence a kind of fowling arises in which it is placed under a net, [III, 15] so that the birds rush upon it. And below: والبوم اصناف وكلها يحب الخلوة بانفسها والتفرد وفي اصل طبعها عداوة الغربان [wa-al-būm aṣnāf wa-kulluhā yuḥibbu al-khalwa bi-anfusihā wa-al-tafarrud wa-fī aṣl ṭabʿihā ʿadāwat al-ghirbān]: Of the album there are several species, all of which love retreat and solitude; but hatred of ravens belongs most of all to their nature. Everyone sees that this is said of the little owl. For the little owl roams by night. The Philosopher, History, book 1, chapter 1: Τὰ μὲν ζῶα νυκτερόβια, οἷον γλαύξ [Ta men zōa nykterobia, hoion glaux]. And from this it has its name. Festus: The noctua is named from the time of night [nox], in which it sings or flies. And Pliny, book 10, chapter 17, describes its skilful fighting against birds; and Aristotle, book 9, chapter 1, its use in fowling: Τῆς δὲ ἡμέρας καὶ τὰ ἄλλα ὀρνίθια τὴν γλαῦκα περιπέτεται, ὃ καλεῖται θαυμάζειν, καὶ προσπετόμενα τέλλουσι. διὸ ὀρνιθοθήραι θηρεύουσιν αὐτῇ παντοδαπὰ ὀρνίθια [Tēs de hēmeras kai ta alla ornithia tēn glauka peripetetai, ho kaleitai thaumazein, kai prospetomena tellousi. dio ornithothērai thēreuousin autē pantodapa ornithia]. By day the other small birds fly around the little owl, which is called admiring, and, flying at it, they pluck it. Therefore fowlers catch small birds of every kind by means of it. Further, on the enmity of the little owl with the crow, which the Arabs designate by the name of raven, see the Philosopher, Pliny and Aelian. Hence arose the proverb in Suidas and [col. 274] Apostolius: Ἄλλο γλαὺξ, ἄλλο κορώνη φθέγγεται ἐπὶ τῶν ἀλλήλοις μὴ συμφωνέντων [Allo glaux, allo korōnē phthengetai epi tōn allēlois mē symphōnentōn]; The little owl sounds one thing, the crow another: said of those who do not agree with each other.
